title: FAAA welcomes AustralianSuper advice expansion but flags levy questions
full_text:
The Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) has welcomed AustralianSuper’s decision to expand financial advice for members, describing the move as recognition of the growing importance of accessible advice while highlighting unresolved regulatory questions around digital advice services.
In a LinkedIn post following AustralianSuper’s announcement of its new advice model, FAAA chief executive Sarah Abood said the fund’s scale made its strategic decisions closely watched across the financial advice sector.
“They’re Australia’s biggest super fund by quite a margin, with over $430 billion in assets and over 3.6 million members. So it’s natural that we watch quite closely what they do.”
Abood said she welcomed the investment in member advice, noting the challenge of delivering advice at scale.
“I’m pleased to see the biggest fund investing in more financial advice for their members. Clearly, they understand how vital advice has become, and it’s no small task to make it available to their millions of members.”
AustralianSuper recently announced it would launch a personalised digital advice platform through a new entity, AustralianSuper Advice, with the service initially covering areas such as investment options, voluntary contributions and retirement planning before expanding over time.
The fund has appointed Quality of Advice Review (QAR) chair Michelle Levy as an independent director of the new advice business.
After reportedly speaking with AustralianSuper to clarify details of the changes, Abood said the most significant development was the introduction of the new digital advice tool, developed in partnership with Ignition Advice and operating under the AustralianSuper Advice licence.
“The biggest development is the introduction of a new digital advice tool for members (partnering with Ignition Advice). The tool will offer intrafund advice to members under a new licence held by AustralianSuper Advice. Starting with quite simple member journeys initially, but getting more fully featured over time.”
While welcoming the development, she said questions had already emerged about whether digital advice services should eventually contribute to industry levies such as those funding ASIC and the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR).
“We’ve fielded questions on whether these digital advice tools will contribute to levies like ASIC, CSLR and so on – and the answer is, at the moment, they don’t. This is something that we’ll need to take a deeper look at, as these tools get more powerful and in future might advise more consumers directly without a human adviser involved.”
Abood also noted Levy’s involvement in the new advice entity, alongside AustralianSuper’s plans to progressively bring its intrafund advice capability in-house.
“The fund will stand up an internal intrafund (human) advice team, over time, working with the digital tools. They will also operate under the new entity AustralianSuper Advice. (The service is currently outsourced to MUFG).”
She said AustralianSuper already employed around 20 intrafund financial advisers, as well as a smaller comprehensive advice team licensed through IFS, with members continuing to be referred to external advisers where appropriate.
More broadly, Abood said the announcement had highlighted ongoing confusion about the advice services superannuation funds can already provide.
“Many super funds have had in-house comprehensive advice teams for years – UniSuper and Aware spring to mind, but there are plenty of others. I’ve been quite surprised at the number of people who weren’t aware that super funds can already offer this service – it’s just that this advice can’t all be collectively charged, in which case members pay individually.”
Looking ahead, Abood said the FAAA was focused on the federal government’s upcoming policy announcements, particularly around CSLR funding and broader advice reforms.
“We’re waiting with bated breath for Minister Dr Daniel Mulino’s announcements next Wednesday at the National Press Club.
“We’re hoping for fixes to CSLR funding, and targeted reforms to stop aggressive lead generation activities aimed at peoples’ super.
“There’s some speculation we might also hear more about the DBFO reforms, which have been stalled for quite a while. We’ll be sending a member alert post the Minister’s speech, with the key announcements and implications,” Abood added.
author: Adrian Suljanovic
